Examples: It was really hot yesterday. The weather was extremely hot yesterday.
Can I say "awesome" in a formal letter?

"Awesome" is a casual word for "very good". In a formal letter, choose "excellent" or "impressive".
Examples: The match was awesome! The school's performance was excellent.
Is "OK" acceptable in an email to my manager?

Yes, "OK" or "okay" is common in work messages, though in a very formal letter you might prefer "agreed" or "that is fine".
Examples: OK, I will send it today. That is fine; I will send the file today.
When is "sufficient" better than "enough"?

"Sufficient" is more formal and suits reports and instructions. "Enough" is the usual word in conversation.
Examples: The funds are sufficient for the repairs. We have enough chairs.
Is "numerous" better than "many" in a report?

"Numerous" is more formal and means "many". In everyday talk, "many" or "a lot of" is more natural.
Examples: The report mentions numerous complaints about the bus service. Many students walk to school.
The class got out of hand when the teacher left. What does that mean?

If something gets out of hand, it becomes too wild or difficult to control.
Example: The noise got out of hand when the whole class started singing at once.
We found a cheap flat near the school, and Dad said we "hit the jackpot". Did we win money?

Not necessarily. To hit the jackpot means to have a big piece of luck or success. It can also mean winning a very large prize.
Example: We hit the jackpot when we found a cheap flat near the school.
What does "by and large" mean in "By and large, the trip was good"?

"By and large" means generally or in most cases.
Example: By and large, the students enjoyed the trip to the museum.
My aunt says my little cousin is "full of beans" today. Is he hungry?

No. To be full of beans means to be lively and full of energy. It is informal and mostly British.
Example: The puppy is full of beans this morning and will not sit still.
Our manager said a new project is "in the pipeline". Where is the pipeline?

There is no real pipeline. If something is in the pipeline, it is being planned or prepared and will happen soon.
Example: A new library is in the pipeline for our town.
My brother says filling in the form twice is "a pain in the neck". Does his neck hurt?

No. A pain in the neck is an informal way to say that something, or someone, is very annoying.
Example: Standing in two queues for one ticket is a pain in the neck.
My cousin is going to "tie the knot" in December. What does that mean?

To tie the knot means to get married.
Example: My cousin will tie the knot in December, and the whole family is invited.
My friends called me a "wet blanket" at the party. What does it mean?

A wet blanket is a person who spoils other people's fun by being gloomy or negative. It is informal.
Example: Don't be a wet blanket, Tara; come and join the game.
When the cart arrived, the kids "made a beeline" for it. Where did they go?

To make a beeline for something means to go straight towards it, without stopping.
Example: The children made a beeline for the ice-cream cart.
I heard "blow up" used for balloons and for an argument. Is that right?

Yes. "Blow up" can mean to fill something with air, to explode, or, informally, to lose your temper suddenly.
Examples: We blew up balloons for the party. Dad blew up when he saw the broken window.
My friend "came down with" a cold before the exam. What does that phrase mean?

To come down with an illness means to start to suffer from it.
Example: Meena came down with a cold the day before the exam.
What does "fill up" mean? The driver said "let's fill up before the highway".

To fill up means to make something completely full, such as a car's fuel tank or a bottle.
Example: Please fill up the water bottle before we start the trek.
I went along with my friends' plan. Does "go along with" mean I walked with them?

Not here. To go along with an idea means to agree to it or accept it. It can also mean to go somewhere together.
Example: I went along with their plan, though I preferred a different route.
What does "knock down" mean? They are going to knock down the old shed.

To knock down a building means to destroy it so that the ground is clear. In shops, it can also mean to reduce a price.
Example: They knocked down the old shed to make room for a garden.
The factory in our town "shut down". What does that phrase mean?

To shut down means to stop operating, either for a time or for ever. It is also used for computers and machines.
Examples: The factory shut down last year. Please shut down the computer before you leave.
Does "wash up" mean the same in British and American English?

No. In British English, "wash up" usually means to wash the dishes after a meal. In American English, it usually means to wash your hands and face.
Example: After dinner, we all helped to wash up.
Could you show me "set aside" in a sentence?

To set something aside means to keep it apart for a special purpose or for later.
Example: Meera sets aside ten minutes every night for reading.
Does "give out" mean to give something away?

It has two meanings. It can mean to hand things to people, and it can mean to stop working or run out.
Examples: The teacher gave out the books. Our old engine finally gave out on the hill.
Do I write "insight" or "incite" in "The book gave me ___ into village life"?

Write "insight", which means a deep understanding of something. "Incite" means to urge people to do something bad or violent.
Examples: The book gave me insight into village life. He was warned not to incite trouble between the neighbours.
Prophecy or prophesy: why do both exist?

They are different parts of speech. "Prophecy", with -cy, is the noun for a statement about the future, and "prophesy", with -sy, is the verb.
Examples: The old prophecy came true. Some storytellers claim to prophesy the future.
Flour or flower: which one goes into chapatis?

"Flour" is the powder from ground grain, used for chapatis and bread. A "flower" is the colourful part of a plant.
Examples: Mix the flour with water to make dough. The flower opened in the morning sun.
I want to "die" my kurta blue. Is that right?

No. Use "dye" for changing the colour of cloth. "Die" means to stop living.
Examples: She dyed the cloth yellow with turmeric. The plant will die without water.
Tale or tail: I want to write about a story.

For a story, write "tale". A "tail" is the part at the back of an animal.
Examples: Grandpa told a tale about a clever crow. The dog wagged its tail.
Is it "scene" or "seen" in "Have you ___ my pen?"

Write "seen". "Seen" is the past participle of "see", and "scene" is a place where something happens or a part of a play.
Examples: Have you seen my pen? The first scene of the play takes place in a market.
Sail or sale: "The shop has a ___ on shoes."

Write "sale", meaning a time when goods are sold cheaply. "Sail" is the cloth on a boat, or the verb for travelling by boat.
Examples: The shop has a sale on shoes. We set sail at dawn.
Hire or higher: "We ___ a car for the trip."

Write "hired". "Hire" means to pay to use something or to employ someone. "Higher" means more high. Americans usually say "rent" for cars.
Examples: We hired a car for the trip to Mysore. The shelf is higher than my head.
Is it "pasttime" or "pastime"?

The correct spelling is "pastime", with only one t in the middle: pas-time.
Example: Reading is her favourite pastime.
Is it oportunity or opportunity?

The correct spelling is "opportunity", with a double p: op-por-tu-ni-ty.
Example: This trip is a good opportunity to practise English.
I wrote "predjudice" in my essay. What is the right spelling?

The correct spelling is "prejudice": pre-ju-dice, with no d before the j.
Example: She had no prejudice against newcomers to the town.
Is "secretery" spelled correctly?

No. The correct spelling is "secretary", ending in -ary: sec-re-tar-y.
Example: The school secretary answered the phone.
Is it sacrafice or sacrifice?

The correct spelling is "sacrifice", ending in -ifice: sac-ri-fice.
Example: He made a sacrifice and gave up his seat to an older woman.
I keep writing "minature". Is that how it's spelled?

No. The correct spelling is "miniature", with an i before the a: min-i-a-ture.
Example: She collects miniature clay animals.
The dark shape of a person against light: silouette or silhouette?

It is "silhouette", with an h after the l: sil-hou-ette.
Example: We saw the silhouette of a tree against the evening sky.
Is "vehical" right?

No. The correct spelling is "vehicle", with a silent h: ve-h-i-cle.
Example: No vehicle may enter the park after dark.
Mould or mold: my science book uses one, my friend's uses the other.

Both are correct. British English spells it "mould" and American English spells it "mold". Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: Mould grew on the old bread.
Catalogue or catalog: which one should I write?

Both are correct. British English usually writes "catalogue" and American English usually writes "catalog", though "catalogue" is also used in the US.
Example: The library has an online catalogue.
Do I write "Monday to Friday" or "Monday through Friday"?

British English usually says "Monday to Friday". American English often says "Monday through Friday". Indian English usually follows the British form.
Example: The office is open Monday to Friday.
Is it "in hospital" or "in the hospital"?

British English usually says "in hospital" when talking about a patient, and American English says "in the hospital". Indian English often follows the British form, but both are heard.
Example: My uncle is in hospital this week, so we visit him every evening.
Do I order a "takeaway" or a "takeout"?

British English says "takeaway", and American English says "takeout". In India, "parcel" is also widely used.
Example: We ordered a takeaway because nobody wanted to cook.
At a restaurant, do I ask for the "bill" or the "check"?

British and Indian English say "the bill". American English usually says "the check".
Example: Could we have the bill, please?
Is it a "ladybird" or a "ladybug"?

British English says "ladybird" and American English says "ladybug".
Example: A ladybird landed on the leaf.
My American cousin says he is "mad at me". Does that mean crazy?

In American English, "mad" usually means angry. In British English, it more often means crazy or very foolish, so "angry" is clearer.
Example: My cousin is mad at me because I forgot his birthday.
Is "request" more formal than "ask"?

Yes. "Request" sounds formal and suits letters and rules. "Ask" is the natural everyday word.
Examples: Students may request extra time in writing. Ask Dad for the keys.
When can I use "prior to" instead of "before"?

"Prior to" is formal and appears in notices and official letters. In everyday speech, "before" is better.
Examples: Please arrive prior to the start of the exam. Wash your hands before lunch.
Should I write "approximately" or "about" in my report?

"Approximately" is more formal and suits reports and exams. "About" is natural in conversation.
Examples: The trip takes approximately three hours. It takes about three hours.
My friend wrote "btw" in a message. What does it stand for?

"BTW" means "by the way". It is an informal short form for messages to friends, not for formal letters.
Example: BTW, I found your pen under the desk.
Can I use "lol" in an email to my teacher?

Better not. "LOL" means "laughing out loud" and is for casual chat with friends. In an email to a teacher, use full sentences.
Examples: Your photo is so funny, lol. That story made me laugh.
Is "folks" a rude word for people?

No. "Folks" is a friendly, informal word for people. In a formal speech, "ladies and gentlemen" or "everyone" fits better.
Examples: Thanks for coming, folks. Good evening, ladies and gentlemen.
Can I call my teacher "dude"?

No. "Dude" is very casual slang, used mostly between close friends. Use "Sir", "Madam" or the teacher's name instead.
Examples: Dude, did you see that catch? Excuse me, Madam, may I ask a question?
In a message to my teacher, can I write "pls" and "thx"?

It is better to write "please" and "thank you" in messages to teachers. Short forms like "pls" and "thx" are for quick chats with friends.
Examples: Pls call me, thx. Please send me the notes. Thank you.
